title: Counting, probability and sets
lines: Counting and probability questions are short to read and easy to get wrong. Before calculating, answer two questions: does order matter, and are items replaced? Then decide whether the complement (counting what you do not want) is quicker.
## The counting principle
- If one choice can be made in m ways and a second, independent choice in n ways, the pair can be made in m × n ways. Extend to any number of stages.
- Handle restrictions first: fill the most limited position before the others.
> An outfit is one of 4 shirts, one of 3 pairs of trousers and one of 2 pairs of shoes. How many outfits?
> A code is 2 letters (repeats allowed) followed by 3 different digits. How many codes?
## Permutations: order matters
- n different items can be arranged in n! ways (5! = 120).
- Choosing and arranging r of n items: n!/(n − r)! = n × (n − 1) × … (r factors).
- With repeated items, divide by the factorial of each repeat count.
- "Must sit together": glue them into one block, arrange the blocks, then arrange inside the block.
> From 8 club members, choose a president, a vice-president and a secretary.
> 8 × 7 × 6 = 336: the roles are different, so order matters.
> How many arrangements of the letters in LEVEL?
> 5 letters with L twice and E twice: 5!/(2! × 2!) = 120/4 = 30.
> Five people sit in a row; Amara and Kwame must sit together. How many seatings?
> Treat the pair as one block: 4 blocks give 4! = 24 orders, times 2 orders inside the pair = 48.
## Combinations: order does not matter
- Choosing r from n with no order: C(n, r) = n!/(r!(n − r)!). C(8, 3) = (8 × 7 × 6)/(3 × 2 × 1) = 56.
- C(n, r) = C(n, n − r): choosing 3 to include is the same as choosing 5 to leave out of 8.
- For "exactly k of one type", multiply the combinations for each group.
> A committee of 3 is chosen from 8 people. How many committees?
> C(8, 3) = 56. The same three people in any order form one committee.
> A team of 4 is chosen from 6 women and 5 men and must contain exactly 2 women. How many teams?
! Test for order: swap two chosen people. If the result is a different outcome (different jobs, seats, ranks), use permutations; if it is the same group, use combinations.
## Basic probability
- P(event) = number of favorable outcomes ÷ number of equally likely outcomes. It lies from 0 to 1.
- P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
- P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). If A and B cannot both happen, the last term is 0.
> Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 8?
> A number is picked at random from 1 to 20. What is the probability it is a multiple of 3 or of 5?
> Multiples of 3: 6. Multiples of 5: 4. Multiples of both (15): 1.
! Count (2,6) and (6,2) separately: the dice are different objects. Treating them as one outcome gives the wrong 3/21.
## Independent and dependent events
- Independent events do not affect each other: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
- Dependent events: after the first event, update the counts. Drawing without replacement is the usual case.
> A coin is tossed and a die is rolled. What is the probability of heads and a 6?
> A bag holds 5 red and 3 blue marbles. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
> First red: 5/8. Second red, with 4 red among 7 left: 4/7.
! With replacement, the second draw would be 5/8 again, giving 25/64. Read whether items go back.
## At least one: use the complement
- P(at least one) = 1 − P(none). Listing the cases one, two, three … is slow and error-prone.
> A player makes each free throw with probability 0.7, independently. In 3 throws, what is the probability of missing at least once?
> P(no misses) = 0.7³ = 0.343, so P(at least one miss) = 1 − 0.343 = 0.657.
> A die is rolled 4 times. What is the probability of at least one six?
> P(no six) = (5/6)⁴ = 625/1,296, so the answer is 671/1,296, about 0.52.
! Adding 1/6 four times gives 4/6, which is wrong: it counts rolls with two sixes twice, and with 7 rolls it would exceed 1.
## Overlapping sets and Venn diagrams
- Two sets: Total = A + B − Both + Neither.
- Three sets: Total = A + B + C − (A∩B + A∩C + B∩C) + (all three) + Neither, where each pairwise count includes the people in all three.
- Draw the circles and fill in from the centre outward: all three first, then pairs, then "only" regions.
> Of 40 students, 25 study French, 18 study Spanish and 7 study neither. How many study both, and how many only French?
> Only French = 25 − 10 = 15.
> In a survey of 100 people, 50 drink tea, 40 coffee and 30 juice. 15 drink tea and coffee, 10 tea and juice, 8 coffee and juice, and 5 drink all three. How many drink none?
! Watch "exactly two" versus "at least two". In the survey, tea and coffee but not juice is 15 − 5 = 10.
## Strategy
- For small cases, list outcomes systematically; on the GRE a careful list of up to 20 items is often fastest.
- For a 2 × 2 problem (for example men/women by left-/right-handed), make a table with totals; every row and column must add up.
- The on-screen calculator helps with products like 26 × 26 × 720, but cancel factorials by hand first: 10!/8! is just 10 × 9 = 90.
